## Working out the components

**Y4 and X4, from X4-Y4-Z2.** Button 1 appears exactly when feature 2 is 1 in both stimuli (for example 1101 0110, 1100 1111, 0100 0111). So **Y4 = bit 2**, **X4 = both are 1**, and **Z2 gives 1 when true, 0 when false**. X4-Y4-Z4 confirms this, giving **Z4: true → 2, false → 3**.

**X3, from X3-Y4-Z2.** On bit 2 the output is 0 only when both bits are 1 (1101 0101, 0111 1100, 1100 1111). Z2 is already fixed, so **X3 = not both are 1**.

**Y3, from X3-Y3-Z2.** The output is 0 exactly when bit 4 is 1 in both stimuli. So **Y3 = bit 4**.

**Y2 and Z1, from X3-Y2-Z1.** Button 3 appears exactly when bit 3 is 1 in both stimuli (1111 0110, 1010 1111, 0010 1010, 0110 1011). So **Y2 = bit 3**, and **Z1 gives 1 when true, 3 when false**.

**Z3, from X5-Y4-Z3.** On bit 2, matching bits (11 or 00) give 0 and differing bits give 2. Two assignments fit all the examples:
- **A:** X5 = "both are the same", and Z3 gives 0 when true, 2 when false.
- **B:** X5 = "exactly one is 1", and Z3 gives 2 when true, 0 when false.

Both are consistent with every known task:
- X5 differs from X3 and X4 under either one.
- Z3 differs from Z1 (1/3), Z2 (1/0) and Z4 (2/3) under either one.

I found no pattern across components that favours one over the other. So the new task is not determined.

## Applying X3-Y2-Z3

The rule is "bit 3 is not 1 in both stimuli". It is false only for inputs 4, 7 and 11.

| Assignment | Rule true (13 inputs) | Rule false (inputs 4, 7, 11) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 2 |
| B | 2 | 0 |

The two assignments disagree on every input. I chose A, which is a coin flip, so my confidence is about 0.5.

```json
{"predictions": [0,0,0,2,0,0,2,0,0,0,2,0,0,0,0,0], "determined": false, "confidence": 0.5}
```

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
